learningObjectives.title: Baroque style and composers (Bach, Handel, Vivaldi)

questions.q: Which dates best define the Baroque period in Western music?
questions.explain: The Baroque period runs from around 1600 to 1750, ending with the death of J.S. Bach.

questions.q: Which Baroque composer wrote the set of violin concertos known as The Four Seasons?
questions.explain: Vivaldi, an Italian composer and priest, wrote The Four Seasons, a famous set of solo violin concertos.

questions.q: Which pair of instruments would typically play a Baroque basso continuo?
questions.explain: The continuo usually combined a chordal instrument such as the harpsichord with a bass instrument such as the cello.

questions.q: Which large-scale choral work is George Frideric Handel best known for?
questions.explain: Handel's oratorio Messiah, containing the 'Hallelujah' chorus, is one of his most celebrated works.

questions.q: In a fugue, what name is given to the main theme first heard on its own at the opening?
questions.explain: A fugue opens with the subject, its principal theme, which is then imitated in other voices.

questions.q: In a concerto grosso, what is the small group of soloists called?
questions.explain: The concertino is the small group of soloists that contrasts with the larger ripieno (full ensemble).

questions.q: What was the nationality of Johann Sebastian Bach?
questions.explain: Bach was a German composer and organist, born in Eisenach in 1685.

questions.q: Which keyboard instrument is most characteristic of the Baroque era?
questions.explain: The harpsichord, whose strings are plucked, was the standard keyboard instrument of the Baroque period.

questions.q: What are 'terraced dynamics'?
options: Sudden changes between loud and soft with little gradual change
Playing every note at the same volume
questions.explain: Terraced dynamics involve abrupt shifts in volume rather than gradual crescendos and diminuendos, suiting instruments like the harpsichord.

questions.q: Which word best describes the texture of a fugue?
questions.explain: A fugue is polyphonic (contrapuntal), weaving together several independent melodic lines at once.

questions.q: What is the main contrast that defines a concerto grosso?
options: A small group of soloists alternating with the full ensemble
A solo singer against a choir
A slow movement followed by a fast one
Loud and soft passages on the organ
questions.explain: The concerto grosso is built on the contrast between the concertino (soloists) and the ripieno (full string ensemble).

questions.q: What is the main function of the basso continuo in Baroque music?
options: To provide a continuous bass line and fill in the harmony
To play the main melody throughout
To double the vocal soprano line
questions.explain: The continuo underpins the music with a steady bass line while the chordal instrument realises the harmony above it.

questions.q: A Baroque suite is best described as which of the following?
options: A collection of contrasting dance movements
A work for solo voice and orchestra
A set of variations on a hymn tune
questions.explain: A suite is a set of stylised dance movements, such as the allemande, courante, sarabande and gigue, usually in the same key.

questions.q: What did the figures (numbers) of a Baroque 'figured bass' tell the continuo player?
options: Which chords to play above the bass notes
questions.explain: Figured bass used numbers beneath the bass line to indicate the intervals and chords to be improvised above it.

questions.q: In a fugue, what is the 'answer'?
options: The subject transposed, usually to the dominant
The final chord of the piece
questions.explain: The answer is the subject restated in another voice, normally transposed up to the dominant key.

questions.q: In Baroque concertos, what happens in 'ritornello' form?
options: A recurring orchestral theme returns between solo episodes
The tempo gradually slows to the end
A single dance is repeated many times
The choir answers the soloist line by line
questions.explain: Ritornello form alternates a returning orchestral theme (the ritornello) with contrasting episodes for the soloist(s).

questions.q: You hear a slow, dignified dance in triple time within a Baroque suite. Which dance is it most likely to be?
questions.explain: The sarabande is a slow, stately dance in triple time, typically placed among the central movements of a suite.

questions.q: In a Baroque work you notice a small group of soloists repeatedly alternating with the full string orchestra. Which genre are you most likely hearing?
questions.explain: Alternation between a small concertino and the full ripieno is the defining feature of the concerto grosso.

questions.q: A Baroque suite ends with a fast, lively dance in compound time (such as 6/8). Which dance is this most likely to be?
questions.explain: The gigue is a quick, energetic dance usually in compound time that traditionally closes a Baroque suite.

questions.q: In a Baroque aria you hear a cello and a harpsichord playing continuous supporting chords beneath the singer. What is this accompaniment called?
questions.explain: A bass instrument plus a chordal keyboard providing continuous harmonic support is the basso continuo.
